posts.post_title: Appliance Maintenance Checklist: Simple Steps to Avoid Costly Repairs in Hobart
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Most of the repair call-outs we see in Hobart trace back to a handful of things that a few minutes of regular maintenance would have prevented — clogged filters, dirty seals, blocked vents and overdue cleans. None of it takes long, and all of it adds years to an appliance's working life.

Fridges & freezers

Vacuum the condenser coils (usually at the back or underneath) every six months, wipe the door seal clean of food residue so it keeps sealing properly, and leave a few centimetres of clearance behind and above the unit for airflow. If you notice it running constantly without getting properly cold, see our guide on what to check if your fridge isn't cooling or freezer not freezing before it becomes a bigger fault.

Washing machines

Clean the pump filter every couple of months — it's usually behind a small panel at the front bottom of the machine — and leave the door ajar between washes so the drum can dry out and avoid mould and odour build-up. Run an empty hot cycle with a machine cleaner every month or so if you mostly wash on cold. Our guides on a machine not draining and making noise cover the most common early warning signs.

Dishwashers

Clean the filter at the bottom of the dishwasher monthly, and run a dishwasher cleaner cycle every couple of months to clear grease and limescale build-up from the spray arms and heating element. If dishes are coming out dirty or the machine won't start, our guides on a dishwasher not cleaning properly and not starting are a good first stop.

Ovens, cooktops & rangehoods

Wipe up spills after they cool rather than letting them bake on at the next use, and run the self-clean function (if fitted) every few months rather than waiting until it's heavily soiled. Clean rangehood grease filters every 2–4 weeks with regular cooking — see our guide on rangehood and cooktop problems for the most common faults this prevents.

Dryers

Clean the lint filter after every single load, not just when you remember — a clogged filter is the leading cause of dryers taking multiple cycles to dry, and a genuine fire risk if ignored for long enough. Have the exhaust duct checked periodically too, since lint builds up there as well over time. See our guide on a dryer not drying clothes properly if you're already noticing longer cycle times.

Vacuums

Empty the bin or bag before it's completely full, clean or replace filters as recommended by the manufacturer, and check the brush roll regularly for tangled hair and thread that restrict its spin. Our guide on a vacuum losing suction covers the most common cause we see.

How often should you actually service major appliances?

  • Fridges & freezers — condenser coil clean every 6 months.
  • Washing machines & dishwashers — filter clean monthly, cleaner cycle every 1–2 months.
  • Dryers — lint filter every load, duct check yearly.
  • Ovens & rangehoods — rangehood filters every 2–4 weeks, oven clean as needed.
  • Anything showing early warning signs (noise, smell, longer cycle times) — worth a look before it becomes a full breakdown.
Almost every "sudden" appliance breakdown we're called out for was actually building up for weeks — a clogged filter, a dirty seal, a blocked vent. Regular maintenance is the cheapest repair you'll ever do.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does regular maintenance actually prevent breakdowns?

Yes — the majority of call-outs we attend for washing machines, dishwashers and dryers trace back to a filter or vent that hasn't been cleaned in a long time, not a genuine component failure.

My appliance is already making a noise or smell — is it too late for maintenance to help?

Not necessarily, but it's worth acting on it now rather than waiting. Early warning signs like noise, smell or slower cycles are usually cheaper to fix the sooner they're addressed.

Do you offer scheduled maintenance visits in Hobart, or only repairs?

We're primarily a repair service, but a maintenance-focused visit can be booked the same way as a repair call-out if you'd like a technician to check an appliance over before it develops a fault.

posts.post_title: Rangehood or Cooktop Not Working? Common Problems and Fixes in Hobart
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A rangehood that won't turn on is usually a tripped switch, a blown fuse, or a failed fan motor, while a cooktop element or burner that won't heat is typically a faulty switch, element, or — on gas — a blocked or misaligned igniter. Both are common, fixable faults rather than reasons to replace the unit outright.

1. Rangehood fan won't turn on at all

Start with the basics: check the isolation switch (often near the rangehood or on a nearby wall) hasn't been switched off, and check the circuit hasn't tripped at the switchboard. If power is confirmed reaching the unit and it still won't start, the fan motor or the control switch itself has likely failed.

2. Rangehood runs but doesn't clear smoke or odours properly

This is almost always a maintenance issue rather than a fault. Grease filters clog with cooking residue over time and choke the airflow — most are dishwasher-safe or can be soaked and scrubbed, and should be cleaned every few weeks with regular cooking. If it's ducted rather than recirculating, a blocked or crushed duct run can also cause weak extraction even with clean filters.

3. Rangehood lights not working

Usually just a blown globe — check the bulb type and wattage before assuming it's electrical. If a freshly replaced globe still doesn't light up, the issue is more likely a faulty light switch or wiring fault.

4. Electric cooktop element not heating

If one element won't heat while the others work fine, the element itself or its dedicated switch has usually failed. If none of the elements work, check the isolation switch and circuit breaker first — a full outage points to power rather than the cooktop itself.

5. Gas cooktop won't ignite or the flame is uneven

A clicking igniter with no spark is often just a burner cap or spark electrode dirty with spilled food — remove and clean both, then dry thoroughly before refitting, since moisture stops the spark reaching the gas. An uneven or yellow (rather than blue) flame usually means the burner ports need a clean, or in some cases a gas supply or regulator issue worth having checked professionally.

When it's a job for a technician

Cleaned the filters and igniter and it's still not working, or you're dealing with anything involving the gas supply, wiring, or a motor replacement — that's where it's worth booking a technician rather than continuing to troubleshoot. Our team repairs rangehoods and both gas and electric cooktops across Hobart, with a flat, upfront quote before any work starts.

Most rangehood "faults" are actually a clogged filter, and most cooktop ignition problems are a dirty burner cap — both are a five-minute clean, not a repair job.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should I clean my rangehood filters?

Every 2–4 weeks with regular home cooking, more often if you cook with a lot of oil or at high heat. A clogged filter is the single biggest cause of weak extraction and is easy to prevent.

Is a clicking gas cooktop with no flame dangerous?

Turn the knob off if it's not igniting after a couple of tries rather than leaving gas flowing while you keep attempting it. Clean the burner and electrode, and if it still won't ignite reliably, have it looked at rather than continuing to force it.

Do you repair both gas and electric cooktops in Hobart?

Yes — we repair gas, electric and induction cooktops, along with ducted and recirculating rangehoods, across Hobart and surrounding suburbs.

Cleaned the filters and burners and still having trouble? Book a technician online for a flat, upfront quote — every repair is backed by our 12-month parts and labour guarantee. See our oven repair Hobart page for more on how we handle kitchen appliance call-outs.

posts.post_title: Microwave Not Heating? Common Problems, Fixes & Whether It's Worth Repairing in Hobart
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A microwave that turns on, spins the turntable and lights up but doesn't actually heat food almost always points to a failed door switch, a blown fuse, or a worn-out magnetron — and whether it's worth repairing usually comes down to the age and price point of the microwave rather than the fault itself.

1. A faulty door interlock switch

Microwaves have safety switches that stop the magnetron firing unless the door is fully closed and latched. If one of these switches wears out or misaligns, the microwave can appear to run normally — light on, turntable spinning, timer counting down — while producing no actual heat, because the safety circuit is silently blocking it. This is one of the more common and relatively affordable fixes.

2. A blown high-voltage fuse

A dedicated fuse protects the high-voltage circuit that powers the magnetron. If it blows — often after a power surge, or simply from age — the microwave keeps running everything else normally but stops producing heat entirely. It's a cheap part, but locating and replacing it safely means opening the unit and working around a capacitor that can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged, which is not a DIY job.

3. A worn-out magnetron

The magnetron is the component that actually generates the microwaves that heat your food. They do wear out with age and heavy use, and replacing one is the most expensive of the common microwave faults — this is usually the point where the repair cost needs to be weighed against a new unit.

4. A faulty diode or capacitor

These two components work together to step up the voltage that drives the magnetron. A failed diode is a relatively inexpensive fix; a capacitor fault needs careful, safe discharging before any work can be done on it, since it can store a serious electrical charge.

5. Turntable spinning but food still cold — is it the same fault?

Not necessarily. A turntable motor issue only affects rotation, not heating — food will still get hot, just unevenly if it isn't rotating. If the turntable is turning normally and the food still isn't heating at all, that points back to the switch, fuse or magnetron faults above rather than the motor.

Is it worth repairing a microwave?

This is genuinely worth thinking through before booking a repair, more so than with most other appliances. A basic microwave is one of the cheaper appliances to replace outright, so a low-cost fix like a door switch or fuse is almost always worth doing, while a magnetron replacement on an entry-level microwave can approach the cost of a new one. A built-in or higher-end combination microwave is a different story — repairing is usually the better call there, since replacement and installation cost considerably more.

If the fault is a switch or a fuse, fix it. If it's the magnetron on a basic benchtop microwave, it's worth asking for a straight comparison against a new unit before you commit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it safe to open my microwave and check the fuse myself?

No — microwaves store a dangerous electrical charge in the high-voltage capacitor even when unplugged, and it isn't something to work on without the right training. Leave anything past checking the door and door seal for damage to a technician.

Why does my microwave make a humming noise but not heat?

A hum with no heat usually points to the magnetron trying to fire and failing, or a high-voltage diode fault. Either way, it needs a proper diagnosis rather than guesswork.

Do you repair built-in and combination microwaves in Hobart?

Yes — we repair benchtop, built-in and combination microwave-ovens across Hobart, and we'll give you an honest opinion on whether a repair or replacement makes more sense for your specific model before any work starts.

posts.post_title: Freezer Not Freezing? 5 Things to Check Before Calling a Repair Tech
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A freezer that's running but not getting properly cold is usually a door seal, ice build-up, or thermostat issue — all things worth checking yourself first. A freezer that's silent and warm right through, or one that's heavily frosted at the back panel, is more likely a sealed system or compressor fault that needs a technician.

1. Check the door seal isn't letting warm air in

A worn, torn or dirty door seal (gasket) is one of the most common reasons a freezer struggles to hold temperature — warm air constantly leaking in forces the compressor to run harder while the freezer still won't get properly cold. Run your hand around the edge of the door while it's closed to feel for drafts, or try the "dollar bill test": close the door on a strip of paper and see if it pulls out easily. Wipe the seal clean of food residue and ice first, since a dirty seal often just needs a clean rather than a replacement.

2. Clear ice build-up from the evaporator and vents

Excess ice can build up around the internal vents or the evaporator coil (usually hidden behind the back panel of the freezer compartment), blocking cold air from circulating properly. If you notice thick ice at the back or top of the compartment, a full defrost — unplug it, leave the door open, and let the ice melt completely — often restores normal freezing before you consider it faulty.

3. Check the temperature setting hasn't been bumped

It sounds obvious, but a dial accidentally knocked while loading groceries, or a digital setting changed by a curious kid, is a genuine and common cause. Most freezers should be set to around -18°C. Give it 24 hours after adjusting the setting before judging whether it's actually fixed the problem, since freezers take time to stabilise.

4. Don't overpack it or block the internal vents

Freezers need air to circulate around the contents to stay cold evenly. Packing it edge-to-edge, or stacking items directly against the back panel where the vents usually sit, can stop cold air reaching the rest of the compartment even though the unit itself is working fine. Leave a little breathing room around the vents, especially at the back.

5. Check the condenser coils and clearance behind the unit

If the freezer is pushed hard against a wall, or the condenser coils underneath or at the back are thick with dust and pet hair, the compressor can't release heat properly and struggles to keep the compartment cold. Pull it out (unplugged), vacuum the coils, and leave a few centimetres of clearance behind and above the unit when you push it back.

When it's a job for a technician

Cleaned the seal, defrosted the ice, checked the setting and cleared the coils and it's still not freezing properly — or the compressor has gone completely silent — that points to a sealed system fault, a failing compressor, or a refrigerant leak, none of which are DIY fixes. Our fridge and freezer repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the exact fault on the visit and give you a flat, upfront price before any work starts.

A freezer that's completely silent and warm right through is a different problem to one that's running constantly but still not cold enough — the first usually means a compressor or power fault, the second usually means airflow or a seal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is my freezer running constantly but not getting cold?

This is the classic sign of a door seal leak, blocked vents, or dirty condenser coils — the compressor is working overtime to compensate but can't win because cold air keeps escaping or can't circulate. Work through the checks above before assuming it's a bigger fault.

How long should I wait after defrosting before deciding it's not fixed?

Give it a full 24 hours after a defrost or a temperature adjustment. Freezers take time to pull back down to temperature, especially if they've been holding warm for a while.

Is it worth repairing an older freezer, or better to replace it?

It usually comes down to the specific fault. A seal, vent blockage or thermostat is a low-cost, worthwhile fix on almost any freezer. A compressor or sealed system fault on an older unit is where it's worth weighing the repair cost against a new one — see our repair or replace decision guide for a straightforward way to think about it.

You might also find our guide on what to check if your fridge isn't cooling useful, since fridge-freezer combo units often share the same causes.

posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Dryer repair cost in Hobart comes down to which part has failed and how much of the machine has to come apart to reach it. A blocked vent, worn door switch or thermal fuse is one of the cheapest fixes there is. A heating element assembly or motor replacement sits at the other end, with more parts and more labour involved. We diagnose the fault first and give you a flat price before any work starts.

What actually drives the cost

Three things decide the final number: how common the fault is, whether the part is already on the van or needs to be ordered in, and how much of the dryer has to be dismantled to reach it. A thermal fuse or door switch is a quick swap. A drum bearing or heating element usually means opening up the cabinet — which is why the price gap between the two can be large, and why nobody can honestly quote a dryer repair sight unseen.

Dryer faults, cheapest to most expensive

  • Lower cost: thermal fuse, door switch, lint filter or vent blockage, drive belt — quick fixes, common parts.
  • Mid cost: drum rollers or bearings, thermostat, idler pulley — more involved access, still straightforward parts.
  • Higher cost: heating element assembly, motor replacement, timer or control board — specialist labour to access and replace.

Is it worth repairing, or should you replace it?

As a rough guide: if the fault sits in the lower or mid range above and the dryer is otherwise in good condition, repairing is almost always the better move — especially backed by a 12-month guarantee. If you're looking at a motor or control board replacement on a dryer that's already well past 8-10 years old, it's worth asking directly whether replacing makes more sense. We'll give you an honest answer either way.

Why we can't just quote a price over the phone

"My dryer isn't drying" and "my dryer stops mid-cycle" can each describe several different faults with very different price points — a dryer that runs but stays cold is a different job to one that overheats and cuts out. That's why every visit starts with a proper diagnosis, then a flat, obligation-free quote before any work begins.

Most Hobart dryer repairs turn out to be the cheaper end of the list above — motor and heating element faults are the exception, not the rule.

It depends entirely on the fault — thermal fuse, door switch and vent issues are inexpensive, drum bearing and thermostat repairs sit in the middle, and heating element or motor work costs the most. We diagnose first and quote a flat price before any work starts.

posts.post_title: How to Choose an Appliance Repair Company in Hobart
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: The fastest way to pick a good appliance repair company in Hobart is to check five things before you book: how they price the job, what guarantee backs the repair, whether they actually service your brand, how they vet their technicians, and what they do if the appliance turns out not to be worth fixing. A company that answers all five clearly, before you commit to anything, is usually a safe bet.

1. Ask how the job is priced — before a technician arrives

Some repairers charge a call-out fee just to look at the appliance, then bill hourly on top of parts. Others diagnose the fault and hand you a single flat price before any work begins, so the number you're quoted is the number you pay. Ask directly: "Is that a flat, all-inclusive price, or could it change once you're here?" A company that can't answer that clearly on the phone is one to be cautious of.

2. Check what guarantee backs the repair

A repair is only as good as what happens if the same fault comes back. Ask specifically whether the guarantee covers both parts and labour, and for how long — a 12-month parts-and-labour guarantee is a reasonable standard to look for. A guarantee that only covers the part, not the labour to fit it again, is worth far less.

3. Confirm they actually work on your brand

Not every repairer services every brand equally well. If you own a less common or higher-end brand, ask directly whether the technician has parts access and experience with it, rather than assuming "appliance repair" covers everything equally.

4. Ask how technicians are vetted

You're letting someone into your home to work on expensive equipment. It's reasonable to ask whether technicians are background-checked and easily identifiable (a uniform, ID, or a marked vehicle) before they arrive — a company with nothing to say here is worth a second thought.

5. Ask what happens if it's not worth repairing

Sometimes a repair genuinely isn't the better option — an old compressor fault on an ageing fridge, for example, can cost more to fix than a replacement is worth. A trustworthy repairer will tell you that honestly during the visit, rather than repairing something anyway because it's billable. If you want to think this through yourself first, our repair-or-replace decision guide walks through the general rule of thumb.

What this looks like in practice

Hobart Appliance Care, for example, quotes a flat, upfront price after diagnosing the fault on-site, backs every repair with a 12-month parts-and-labour guarantee, and uses background-checked, uniformed technicians. It's a reasonable checklist to hold any local repairer to, not just this one — but it's also exactly what you can expect if you book a repair online or get in touch directly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I get more than one quote?

For a straightforward, common fault it's usually not necessary if the company gives you a flat price after diagnosis — you're not committing to anything until you've seen the number. It's more worthwhile for a big-ticket repair (like a compressor or control board) where you're already weighing repair against replacement.

What questions should I avoid skipping?

The pricing structure and the guarantee are the two most commonly glossed over — ask both explicitly, even if the rest of the call feels straightforward.

Does a lower call-out price always mean a better deal?

Not necessarily. A low call-out fee attached to an hourly rate can end up costing more than a slightly higher flat, all-inclusive price — check what's actually included before comparing numbers.

posts.post_title: Repair or Replace? A Decision Guide for Hobart Homeowners
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: As a rough industry rule of thumb, if a repair quote comes in under about half the cost of a new equivalent appliance, and the appliance is not already old or unreliable, repairing is usually the better financial call. Above that, or if it has already been repaired more than once, replacing tends to make more sense. The right answer always depends on the actual fault — which is why we diagnose first and give you an honest opinion either way.

The 50% rule of thumb

It is a commonly used guideline, not a strict formula: compare the repair quote to the cost of a new, similar-spec appliance. Well under half suggests repair. Getting close to, or over, half suggests it may be time to replace — especially once you factor in the appliance’s age and how many times it has already needed attention.

How long should your appliance actually last?

Typical expected lifespans (with reasonable care) look roughly like this:

  • Fridges: around 10–15 years
  • Washing machines: around 8–12 years
  • Dishwashers: around 8–10 years
  • Ovens: around 12–15 years
  • Dryers: around 10–13 years
  • Vacuums: around 5–8 years, depending on use and type

An appliance failing well before this range might point to a manufacturing issue or hard use, and is often still worth repairing. One failing near or past this range is more often a sign that a second or third repair is coming soon.

Signs it is time to replace, not repair

  • This is the second or third repair in a short period
  • The quoted repair is close to, or more than, half the cost of a new equivalent model
  • The appliance is already at or past its typical lifespan
  • Newer models offer a meaningful efficiency or capacity upgrade you actually need
  • Replacement parts are hard to source or discontinued

Signs it is worth repairing

  • The appliance is younger than its typical lifespan
  • The fault is a common, lower-cost one — a seal, belt, filter or switch, rather than a motor or control board
  • It has not needed a repair before
  • You are otherwise happy with its performance, capacity and features

Why an honest diagnosis matters more than a rule of thumb

Rules of thumb are a starting point, not a substitute for actually knowing what is wrong. A fridge that sounds like a major fault might just need a $-cheap thermostat; a dishwasher on its third "minor" repair might be signalling a bigger problem underneath. That is why every Hobart Appliance Care visit starts with a proper diagnosis and a flat, upfront quote — so the repair-or-replace decision is based on your actual appliance, not a guess.

posts.post_title: Vacuum Keeps Shutting Off? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A vacuum that keeps cutting out mid-clean is almost always its built-in overheating protection reacting to blocked airflow — a full bin, a clogged filter, or a blocked hose or brush roll — rather than a serious fault. Clear those and give it time to cool down before assuming it needs a repair.

1. Empty the bin or check the bag

A full bin or bag is the most common reason a vacuum overheats and shuts off. It restricts airflow through the motor, and the built-in thermal protection cuts power to protect it — often before the bin even looks completely full.

2. Clean or replace the filter

A clogged filter has the same effect as a full bin — it chokes airflow through the motor. Most filters can be rinsed (check they're fully dry before refitting) or should be replaced roughly every three to six months depending on how often you vacuum.

3. Check the hose and brush roll for blockages

Hair, string and larger debris can lodge in the hose or wrap around the brush roll, restricting airflow the same way a full bin does. Detach the hose if possible and check for anything stuck along its length.

4. Let it cool down before restarting

Once the thermal cutout trips, most vacuums need somewhere around 30–45 minutes to cool before they'll run properly again. Switching it straight back on repeatedly won't fix the underlying blockage and can trip the cutout again immediately.

5. Check the power cord and plug

A vacuum that cuts out intermittently rather than after sustained use, particularly if it flickers on and off when the cord is moved, may have a frayed cord or a loose connection at the plug rather than an airflow issue.

When it's a job for a technician

Emptied the bin, cleaned the filter, checked the hose, and it's still shutting off after cooling down properly? That points to a motor or wiring fault that needs proper diagnosis. Our vacuum repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the exact cause on the visit and give you a flat, upfront price before any work starts.

A vacuum that keeps overheating even with a clear bin, filter and hose usually points to the motor itself — not something left blocking the airflow.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long should I wait before turning the vacuum back on?

Give it 30–45 minutes to cool down fully. Turning it back on too soon after the cutout trips can trigger it again straight away, even once the blockage is cleared.

Is overheating protection a fault, or is it supposed to happen?

It's a normal safety feature designed to protect the motor — it's only a sign of a fault if it keeps happening even with a clear bin, clean filter and unblocked hose.

How much does this kind of repair typically cost?

It depends on the fault — a filter or hose issue costs nothing to fix yourself, while a motor fault costs more. We diagnose and quote upfront before any work starts, and every repair is backed by a 12-month parts and labour guarantee.

posts.post_title: Dryer Stopping Mid-Cycle? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A dryer that stops partway through a cycle is almost always a built-in safety cutoff reacting to restricted airflow — a clogged lint filter, a blocked vent hose, or an overloaded drum — rather than a major fault. If it keeps happening after you've cleared all three, the thermal fuse itself may have failed.

1. Clean the lint filter

A clogged lint filter is the single most common reason a dryer overheats and cuts out early. It should be cleaned before every load, not just when it looks full — a thin, invisible layer of lint can restrict airflow enough to trip the safety cutoff even when the filter looks reasonably clear.

2. Check the vent hose isn't blocked or crushed

The hose running from the back of the dryer to the outside vent can get crushed if the machine has been pushed back against a wall, or slowly clog with lint over months of use. Pull the dryer out and check the hose runs freely, with no kinks or flat sections restricting airflow.

3. Don't overload the drum

A drum packed too full restricts how air circulates around the clothes, which can be enough to trip the same thermal safety cutoff as a blocked vent. Splitting a large load into two smaller ones is worth trying if this keeps happening.

4. Give it time to cool down between attempts

If the safety cutoff has tripped, some dryers need 30–45 minutes to cool before they'll start again. Restarting it repeatedly straight after it cuts out won't fix the underlying airflow issue and can just trip the cutoff again immediately.

5. Check the door is closing firmly

A door that isn't latching firmly, or a door switch that's come slightly loose, can cause the dryer to stop mid-cycle even though nothing else is wrong. Close the door firmly and listen for a solid click.

When it's a job for a technician

Cleared the filter, checked the vent, and it's still cutting out — or cutting out consistently at the same point every cycle? That points to a failed thermal fuse, thermostat or door switch that needs proper diagnosis. Our dryer repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the exact cause on the visit and give you a flat, upfront price before any work starts.

A dryer that keeps cutting out even with a clean filter and clear vent usually means the safety fuse itself has failed — and that's a part swap, not a cleaning job.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it safe to keep using a dryer that keeps shutting off?

It's the appliance protecting itself from overheating, so it's not unsafe in the moment — but repeatedly restarting it without fixing the underlying airflow issue puts extra strain on the motor and heating element over time.

How often should I clean the vent hose, not just the filter?

Roughly every six months for most households, or more often if you dry heavily or have a longer duct run to the outside vent.

How much does a thermal fuse or vent repair typically cost?

It depends on the fault — a thermal fuse is generally an affordable fix. We diagnose and quote upfront before any work starts, and every repair is backed by a 12-month parts and labour guarantee.

posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A dishwasher that won't start at all is most often the door not latching properly, a control lock switched on by accident, or a tripped circuit — all quick to check yourself. If the door latches fine, power's confirmed, and it still won't start, that's usually a door switch or control board fault.

1. Check the door is latching properly

Most dishwashers have a safety switch that stops the cycle from starting unless the door is fully closed and latched. Open and firmly close the door again — sometimes an item leaning against the door, or a rack pulled out slightly too far, is enough to stop it from clicking shut properly.

2. Check for a control lock or child lock

Many models have a control lock (sometimes labelled with a small padlock icon) that can be switched on by accident, especially in a busy kitchen. Check your model's manual for the button combination to unlock it — it's a common, easy fix that looks exactly like a dead machine until you know what to look for.

3. Check the power supply

If the display shows a countdown or a time rather than starting the cycle immediately, a delay start has likely been set — accidentally or otherwise. Cancelling it and starting the cycle fresh usually sorts it.

posts.post_title: Oven Making Noise? Here's What It Means
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Most oven noises are completely normal — metal expanding as it heats, a fan spinning up, or an igniter clicking a few times before it lights. It's worth a closer look when a noise is new, repeats every cycle, or gets louder — that usually points to a fan motor, igniter or bearing issue rather than just the oven warming up.

Kitchen appliance trouble isn't limited to the oven itself — see our guide on rangehood and cooktop problems if that's what's playing up.

1. A gentle humming or fan noise

Fan-forced ovens run a convection fan any time that mode is on, so a steady, even hum is completely normal. It's worth a look if the fan has suddenly gotten noticeably louder, or if you hear it rattling rather than humming — that can mean something loose, or a bit of food debris, has made contact with the fan blade.

2. Clicking when it's heating up

On gas ovens, a series of clicks as the igniter tries to light the burner is completely normal, and should stop once it catches. If it clicks repeatedly without ever lighting, or the clicking continues throughout cooking, the igniter itself may be failing. On electric ovens, an occasional click as the thermostat cycles the element on and off is also normal.

3. Popping or banging sounds

A pop or two as the oven heats up is usually just the metal cavity and racks expanding — harmless, and very common in the first few minutes of preheating. Frequent, loud banging throughout cooking is less typical and worth mentioning to a technician, especially if it's new.

4. A loud or grinding fan

A grinding or whining sound specifically from the fan, especially if it changes pitch or gets worse over time, usually points to a worn fan motor bearing rather than anything blocking the blade. This one tends to get worse rather than better on its own.

5. Buzzing that doesn't stop

A short buzz as an element or igniter engages is normal. A constant buzz that continues for the whole cook, particularly alongside uneven heating, can point to a failing element or control board rather than just normal operating noise.

When it's a job for a technician

If a noise is new, gets louder over time, or comes with another symptom like uneven cooking or the oven not heating properly, it's worth getting it looked at before a small fan or igniter issue turns into something bigger. Our oven repair technicians in Hobart diagnose gas and electric ovens on the visit, with a flat, upfront price before any work begins.

A grinding fan rarely fixes itself — bearings wear gradually, and the noise almost always gets worse rather than better over time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for a new oven to make noise?

Some clicking, humming and the odd pop while heating is normal on both new and older ovens. What's not normal is a noise that's constant, grinding, or getting louder each time you use it.

Can I keep using the oven if it's making noise?

For a mild hum or occasional click, yes. If you're hearing grinding, loud banging, or a burning smell alongside the noise, it's safer to stop using it and get it checked.

posts.post_title: Washing Machine Not Draining? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A washing machine that fills and washes but won't drain is almost always a blockage somewhere in the drain path — the pump filter, the drain hose, or the external standpipe — rather than a serious fault. A drain pump that hums but doesn't shift water is the one that usually needs a technician.

1. Clean out the pump filter

Most front loaders have a small access panel near the bottom front of the machine hiding a pump filter (sometimes called a coin trap). Coins, buttons, hair ties and lint collect here over time and are one of the most common reasons a machine stops draining. Have a shallow tray ready — there's usually some water behind it — then unscrew it, clear it out, and refit it firmly.

2. Check the drain hose for kinks

If the machine has been pushed back against a wall or moved recently, the drain hose can end up kinked or squashed behind it, which stops water getting through even though everything inside the machine is working fine. Pull the machine out slightly and check the hose runs freely from the back of the machine to the drain point.

3. Check the external drain point isn't blocked

The standpipe or laundry drain the hose empties into can block with lint and detergent residue over time, especially in older plumbing. If water backs up or drains very slowly from the laundry sink or floor drain generally, the blockage is downstream of the machine rather than in it.

4. Don't overload the machine

A very heavy, tightly packed load can unbalance the drum and, on some machines, trigger a safety lock that pauses the cycle before draining. Splitting a large load into two smaller ones is worth trying if this happens repeatedly.

5. Listen for the drain pump itself

If you can hear a humming or buzzing sound during the drain stage but no water is actually leaving the machine, the drain pump motor or impeller has likely failed or is jammed — often by a sock, coin or small item that's made it past the filter. This isn't a DIY fix on most machines, since it usually means partially dismantling the unit.

When it's a job for a technician

Cleared the filter and hose and it's still not draining, or you can hear the pump trying and getting nowhere? That's a drain pump or wiring fault. Our washing machine repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the exact cause on the visit and give you a flat, upfront price before any work starts.

A machine that hums during the drain cycle but never actually empties is almost always a pump problem — not a blockage you can clear yourself.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it safe to keep using the machine if it won't drain?

Avoid running further loads until it's sorted — standing water left in the drum can start to smell, and running a blocked machine repeatedly can put extra strain on the pump if it's already struggling.

Can I clean the pump filter myself?

Yes — it's designed to be user-accessible on most machines, and clearing it is one of the quickest ways to solve a draining issue yourself before booking a technician.

posts.post_title: Fridge Not Defrosting? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Ice building up inside a fridge or freezer instead of clearing on its own usually means the automatic defrost cycle isn't running properly — most often a worn door seal letting warm, moist air in, a blocked drain tube, or a failed defrost heater or thermostat that should be melting frost off the coils every few hours. A couple of these you can rule out yourself; a heater or thermostat fault needs a technician.

1. Check the door seal

A worn or gappy door seal (gasket) lets warm, humid room air leak into the fridge or freezer continuously, and that moisture is exactly what turns into ice inside. Close the door on a piece of paper — if it pulls out easily, the seal isn't holding. Wipe the gasket down with warm soapy water first, since a sticky, grimy seal often just needs a clean rather than replacing.

2. Clear the drain tube

Every defrost cycle melts a small amount of frost off the coils, and that water is meant to run down a drain tube (usually at the back of the freezer or fridge compartment) into a tray underneath. If that tube is blocked with food debris or ice, the meltwater has nowhere to go — it refreezes inside the cabinet instead of draining away, and you'll often see water pooling at the bottom of the fridge as well as ice building up.

3. Don't overpack or block the internal vents

Fridges and freezers have small air vents that circulate cold air between compartments. Food packed hard up against a vent restricts that airflow, and the cold, damp air tends to condense and freeze right around the blockage — which shows up as a patch of ice in the same spot every time.

4. Do a full manual defrost and watch what happens next

If ice has already built up thick, switch the fridge off, empty it, and let it thaw completely (towels down to catch the water — this usually takes several hours to overnight). Once it's back up and running, keep an eye on it for a few days. Ice that comes back slowly, over a week or two, points to a seal or vent issue. Ice that starts building back within a day or two points to something in the defrost system itself.

5. Listen for the automatic defrost cycle

Most fridges run a short automatic defrost cycle a few times a day — you might hear a faint hum or notice slight warming inside for a few minutes. If you never notice any change and the ice just keeps thickening no matter what, the defrost heater or thermostat has most likely stopped working, and no amount of manual defrosting will fix that for good.

When it's a job for a technician

If the seal, drain and vents all check out fine and the ice keeps coming back quickly even after a full defrost, you're almost certainly looking at a defrost heater, thermostat or timer fault. These sit inside the freezer compartment alongside live electrical components, so it's not a safe DIY job. Our fridge repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the exact cause on the visit and give you a flat, upfront price before any repair work starts.

Ice that builds back within a day or two, even right after a full defrost, is a heater or thermostat fault — not a seal problem, and manual defrosting will only ever be a temporary fix.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is some frost in the freezer normal?

A thin layer that builds up gradually over a few weeks and clears during the normal defrost cycle is completely normal. Thick ice that returns within a day or two of clearing it is not, and points to a genuine fault.

Can I just keep manually defrosting it instead of getting it repaired?

You can for a while, but it's a losing battle if the heater or thermostat has actually failed — the fridge has to work harder to stay cold around the ice buildup, which is worse for the compressor and your power bill in the meantime.

It depends on which part has failed — a heater or thermostat is generally more affordable than a control board. See our appliance repair cost guide for what typically affects the price, or we'll diagnose and quote upfront before any work starts.

Yes — every repair we carry out is backed by a 12-month parts and labour guarantee, so if the same fault recurs within that period, it's covered.

posts.post_title: Dyson Vacuum Repair Hobart: Common Problems & Fixes
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: The three Dyson faults we see most in Hobart are lost suction (almost always a filter or blockage issue), a cordless model not holding charge (usually the battery, not the motor), and a brush bar that's stopped spinning (tangled hair or a worn belt). All three are genuine, worthwhile repairs — not a sign the vacuum is finished.

Losing suction — check the filters and bin first

Dyson filters need washing every month or so (check your model — most are rinse-in-cold-water, air-dry-fully, no detergent), and a full bin or a cyclone clogged with fine dust will drop suction noticeably before you'd expect. Wash the filter, empty and check inside the bin and cyclone assembly, and let the filter dry completely before refitting — a damp filter is a common cause of suction that seems to never fully recover.

Cordless Dyson not holding charge

On V-series and similar cordless models, the battery is a separate, replaceable unit — not soldered into the motor. A battery that drains in a couple of minutes, or won't charge past one bar, is a battery fault, not a sign the whole machine needs replacing. It's genuinely one of the more affordable Dyson repairs.

Brush bar not spinning

Same underlying causes as any vacuum — hair and thread wound tightly around the bar, or a worn drive belt — but Dyson's brush bar housing typically clips off for cleaning without tools, making it one of the easier checks to do yourself before booking anything.

High-pitched noise or the machine cutting out

A rising, high-pitched whine usually means the motor is struggling against a blockage somewhere in the airway — check the hose and wand for anything lodged inside, not just the bin. A Dyson that cuts out mid-clean and won't restart straight away has likely hit its thermal cut-out from overheating; let it cool for 20-30 minutes before trying again.

Why genuine parts matter

Dyson's cyclone and filtration system is precisely engineered — a cheap aftermarket filter or an ill-fitting third-party battery can genuinely cost you suction performance even when it "fits". We use genuine or manufacturer-equivalent parts so the repair actually restores the vacuum to how it's meant to perform.

If you've washed the filters, cleared the airway and checked the brush bar but the fault's still there, it's time for a proper diagnosis rather than guessing further. Our vacuum repair technicians in Hobart service Dyson and most major brands, with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A Dyson losing performance is rarely the motor giving up — in our experience it's the filter, the battery or a blockage in nine cases out of ten.

posts.post_title: Vacuum Brush Roll Not Spinning? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A vacuum brush roll that's stopped spinning is most often tangled hair or thread wrapped around it, or a worn drive belt that's lost its grip. Both are quick, inexpensive fixes. If the brush stopped mid-clean rather than never starting, a safety cut-out from overheating is another common cause.

1. Check for tangled hair and thread

Hair, thread and carpet fibres wind tightly around the brush roll over time until it can no longer spin freely, forcing the motor to strain against it. Turn the vacuum over, remove the brush roll cover, and cut away tangled material carefully with scissors — this alone resolves a large share of "brush not spinning" cases.

2. Check the drive belt

If the brush roll turns freely by hand but won't spin on its own, the belt connecting it to the motor has likely stretched, slipped, or snapped. A loose belt often lets the motor run while the brush stays still — listen for the motor sound without the usual brush noise as a clue.

3. Check the brush roll bearings

Hair and debris can also work into the bearings at each end of the brush roll, not just the bristles themselves, adding enough resistance to stop it turning even once the visible tangles are cleared. Check both ends of the roll, not just the middle.

4. Check the hard-floor or brush-off setting

Many vacuums have a setting that deliberately stops the brush roll for use on hard floors or delicate rugs. Double-check this hasn't been left on by accident — it's an easy thing to overlook and looks identical to a fault.

5. Check for a tripped safety cut-out

If the brush was spinning normally and then stopped mid-clean, the motor may have hit a safety cut-out from overheating — usually triggered by the exact tangles or blockages above making it work too hard. Clear any obstructions, switch off, and let it cool for 20–30 minutes before trying again.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've cleared tangles, checked the belt and bearings and the brush roll still won't spin, it's likely a worn brush motor or a drive mechanism fault that needs a proper diagnosis. Our vacuum repair technicians in Hobart service most major brands, including Dyson, with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A belt is one of the cheapest parts on a vacuum to replace — worth ruling out before assuming a brush roll fault means a new machine.

Why did my vacuum's brush roll suddenly stop spinning?

Most often it's tangled hair or thread that's built up gradually until the brush finally seizes, or a belt that's finally slipped or snapped after months of wear — it usually feels sudden even though the cause built up over time.

Is replacing a vacuum belt an easy fix?

Yes, on most models it's an inexpensive part and a straightforward job once the brush roll cover is off — one of the cheapest vacuum repairs there is.

posts.post_title: Oven Door Won't Close? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: An oven door that won't close properly is usually a worn or dirty door gasket, a bent hinge, or a latch that isn't catching correctly. Even a small gap lets heat escape, which wastes power and can cause uneven cooking — it's worth checking before you assume the whole door needs replacing.

1. Check the door gasket for damage or debris

Run your hand around the rubber or fibreglass seal for cracks, tears, or sections that have come loose. Food splatter and grease build-up can also stop the gasket sitting flush — wipe it down with warm soapy water and check again before assuming it needs replacing.

2. Check the hinges

Open and close the door slowly and watch how it sits — a door that sags or sits crooked usually points to a bent or loose hinge. Over years of use, hinge springs can also weaken, leaving the door not pulling fully shut under its own weight.

3. Check the door latch

Some ovens use a latch that can bend slightly out of position over time, effectively propping the door open a few millimetres. Check the latch moves freely and lines up with its catch when the door is closed.

4. Check nothing's blocking the door

A rack pushed in slightly crooked, a tray that's slid forward, or a stray oven mitt can all physically stop the door from closing fully. Open the oven and check every rack and tray is pushed all the way back and sitting level.

5. Check the door sits flush all the way around

With the door closed, look at the gap between the door and the oven frame on all four sides — top, bottom and both sides. An even gap suggests a gasket problem; a gap that's only on one side points more towards a hinge or frame alignment issue.

When it's a job for a technician

If the gasket's clean and intact, the hinges look straight and nothing's blocking it but the door still won't sit flush, it's likely a hinge or frame alignment fault that needs a proper diagnosis. Our oven repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A door that isn't sealing doesn't just waste power — it's one of the most common hidden causes of an oven that bakes unevenly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is my oven door not sitting flush against the frame?

This is most often a worn or dirty door gasket, or a hinge that's bent or loosened over time. Check the gasket first — it's the easiest thing to inspect and the most common cause.

Does a gap in the oven door waste a lot of power?

Yes — the oven has to run its heating element more often to make up for the heat escaping, which shows up as higher power use and an oven that takes longer to reach temperature.

posts.post_title: Dishwasher Not Cleaning Dishes Properly? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Dishes coming out cloudy, greasy or still dirty usually comes down to one of five things: no rinse aid, a blocked filter, hard water build-up, dishes blocking the spray arms, or water that isn't running hot enough. None of them mean the dishwasher itself is broken — all are worth checking before booking a repair.

1. Check the rinse aid

Rinse aid is what stops water beading and drying into cloudy spots on glasses and cutlery — without it, even a perfectly working dishwasher leaves dishes looking dull. Check the dispenser is topped up and the cap is clicked shut properly, not just sitting loosely on top.

2. Check the filter

Most dishwashers have a removable filter at the bottom of the tub that needs clearing out every few weeks. A filter clogged with food scraps restricts water flow to the spray arms, leaving dishes only partially cleaned. Pull it out, rinse it under a tap, and refit it firmly.

3. Check for hard water build-up

A cloudy film that won't wipe off (as opposed to spots that do) is usually limescale from hard water rather than a cleaning fault. Run an empty cycle with a cup of white vinegar in the bottom of the tub — if the film noticeably improves, hard water build-up is the cause, not the machine.

4. Check you're not blocking the spray arms

Large plates, trays or overcrowded racks can physically block the spray arms from reaching every dish, or stop the arms spinning freely. Load with soiled sides facing inward, and spin each spray arm by hand before starting a cycle to make sure nothing's in its way.

5. Check the water is running hot enough

Dishwasher detergent needs genuinely hot water to dissolve and work properly — if the kitchen tap runs lukewarm before it heats up, the dishwasher may be starting its cycle before hot water reaches it. Run the kitchen sink tap until it's hot immediately before starting the dishwasher to help.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've topped up rinse aid, cleared the filter, ruled out hard water and checked loading but dishes are still coming out dirty, it's likely a spray arm, wash pump or heating fault that needs a proper diagnosis. Our dishwasher repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

Most "my dishwasher stopped cleaning properly" calls turn out to be maintenance, not a mechanical fault — a five-minute filter clean fixes more of these than people expect.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are my glasses coming out of the dishwasher cloudy?

This is almost always missing rinse aid or hard water mineral build-up, not a fault with the dishwasher. Top up the rinse aid first, then try the vinegar rinse test if the cloudiness doesn't clear.

Is hard water build-up something a technician needs to fix?

No — it's a water-quality issue, not a mechanical fault, and usually clears with regular vinegar rinses or a rinse-aid dose increase. A technician is only needed if dishes stay dirty after ruling out rinse aid, hard water and a blocked filter.

posts.post_title: Washing Machine Making Noise? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A washing machine that bangs loudly during the spin cycle is most often an unbalanced load or a machine that's come out of level. Grinding or rumbling instead of banging points to worn drum bearings or shock absorbers, and is worth getting checked rather than run through more loads.

1. Check for an unbalanced load

Heavy items like towels, doonas or jeans can clump together on one side of the drum, throwing it off balance enough to bang against the cabinet at high spin speeds. Open the machine and redistribute the load evenly, or split a large load into two smaller ones.

2. Check the machine is level

A washing machine that rocks on the floor will bang far more than one sitting flat. Use a spirit level across the top and adjust the feet until it doesn't rock when you push down on each corner.

3. Check nothing's caught between the drum and the outer tub

Coins, bra underwires, buttons and other small items can work loose from pockets and get trapped between the inner drum and outer tub, causing a sharp banging or clanking with every rotation. This usually needs the machine opened up to retrieve, though it's worth checking pockets before every wash to prevent it.

4. Check the shock absorbers (front-loaders)

Front-loading machines use shock absorbers to dampen the drum's movement during spin. As these wear out over the years, the drum starts swinging further than it should and banging against the cabinet. If the noise has gradually gotten worse over months, worn shocks are a likely cause.

5. Grinding or rumbling — stop and get it checked

A grinding or rumbling noise, rather than a bang, usually means the drum bearings have worn out and need replacing. Continuing to run the machine in this state can let the drum sit unevenly and eventually damage the outer tub, turning a bearing job into a bigger repair.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've rebalanced the load and confirmed the machine is level but it's still banging — or you're hearing grinding rather than banging — it's likely a worn shock absorber, drum bearing or suspension spring, and that's a job for a qualified technician. Our washing machine repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A banging washing machine rarely fixes itself — left running, worn suspension components put extra strain on the motor and drum bearings too.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my washing machine only bang during the spin cycle?

Banging is almost always tied to spin speed — the drum spins fastest during the spin cycle, so an unbalanced load or worn suspension component only becomes noticeable (and loud) at that point, even though the fault is there throughout the wash.

Is it safe to keep using a washing machine that bangs?

For an occasional bang from an unbalanced load, yes. But regular, worsening banging usually means a suspension or bearing fault, and continuing to run it risks further damage to the drum and tub — worth getting checked sooner rather than later.

It depends on the fault — a levelling or load issue costs nothing to fix yourself, while a shock absorber or bearing replacement costs more. See our appliance repair cost guide for what typically affects the price, or we'll diagnose and quote upfront before any work starts.

posts.post_title: Vacuum Won't Turn On? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A vacuum with no power at all is usually one of a few things: for corded models, check the outlet, cord and circuit breaker first; for cordless models, it's almost always the battery or charging dock. A tripped thermal cut-out from overheating is another common, easily-missed cause on both types.

1. Check the outlet and plug connection

It sounds obvious, but test the outlet with another device (phone charger, lamp) before assuming the vacuum itself has failed. Push the plug in firmly — a loose connection at the wall is a surprisingly common cause of an intermittent "no power" fault.

2. Check the power cord for damage

Inspect the full length of the cord for cuts, fraying or a chewed section (pets are a common culprit), and check both ends — where it meets the plug and where it enters the vacuum body — for a loose or damaged connection.

3. Check the circuit breaker

A vacuum drawing a sudden high load (especially on an older circuit) can trip a breaker without any other warning sign. Check your switchboard and reset if needed, then try a different outlet on a different circuit if it trips again.

4. Cordless vacuums: check the battery and dock

Confirm the battery is actually charging — look for a charging light on the dock or handle, and try leaving it on charge for a full cycle rather than assuming a quick check is enough. A dock that isn't seated properly, or contacts with a build-up of dust, can stop charging even though everything looks connected.

5. Check for a tripped thermal cut-out

Most vacuums have a safety cut-out that shuts the motor off if it overheats — often triggered by a blocked filter, full bin or clogged hose making the motor work too hard. If the vacuum stopped mid-clean rather than failing to start at all, switch it off, clear any blockages, and let it cool for 30–45 minutes before trying again.

When it's a job for a technician

If the outlet, cord, breaker and (for cordless models) battery all check out and the vacuum still won't power on, it's likely a faulty switch or an internal wiring fault that needs a proper diagnosis. Our vacuum repair technicians in Hobart service most major brands, including Dyson, with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A vacuum that cuts out repeatedly from overheating is worth getting checked even if it eventually powers back on — it's usually a sign of an ongoing blockage or an ageing motor working harder than it should.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did my vacuum stop working suddenly mid-clean?

This points more towards a thermal cut-out than a power fault — the motor has likely overheated from a blockage or full bin and shut itself off as a safety measure. Let it cool and clear any blockages before trying again.

Is it worth repairing a cordless vacuum with a dead battery?

Usually, yes — on most models the battery is a separate, replaceable part rather than something built into the motor, so a battery replacement is generally far cheaper than a new vacuum.

posts.post_title: Dryer Making Noise? Here’s What It Means
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A squealing or squeaking dryer usually points to a worn idler pulley or drum roller bearing. Thumping or banging is more often an unbalanced load or a flat-spotted roller from the dryer sitting unused. A grinding metal-on-metal noise is more serious and worth stopping the dryer for until it's checked.

1. Squealing or squeaking

This is almost always a rotating part that's worn or no longer running smoothly — usually the idler pulley that keeps tension on the drive belt, or one of the drum support rollers. Both wear gradually and get louder over time rather than appearing suddenly, so if it's been building for a few weeks, this is the likely cause.

2. Thumping or banging during the cycle

A single heavy item, or bedding like sheets and doonas that bunch into a ball, will thump against the drum as it tumbles — try splitting a large load into two smaller ones. If the noise happens on every load regardless of what's in it, a flat spot on a drum roller (common after the dryer's sat unused for a while) is a more likely cause.

3. Check nothing's caught inside the drum

Coins, buttons, bra underwires and other small items can work their way out of pockets and get caught between the drum and the cabinet, causing a rattling or clunking sound. Run the drum by hand (dryer unplugged) and check around the drum seal for anything stuck.

4. Check the dryer is level

An unlevel dryer can rock slightly during the cycle, which sometimes sounds like a deeper structural noise. Use a spirit level on top and adjust the feet until it sits flat and doesn't rock when pushed.

5. Grinding noise — stop and get it checked

A grinding, metal-on-metal sound usually means a drum roller or bearing has worn through completely, letting metal parts rub directly against each other. Continuing to run the dryer at this point can damage the drum itself, turning a simple roller replacement into a much bigger repair.

When it's a job for a technician

If the noise is a squeal that's getting louder, a thump that happens on every load, or anything that sounds like grinding, it's time to get it looked at rather than waiting for it to fail completely. Our dryer repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A squealing or thumping dryer rarely fixes itself — left running, a worn roller or bearing usually leads to a bigger repair, not a smaller one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did my dryer suddenly start squealing?

It's rarely truly sudden — a worn idler pulley or drum roller usually squeaks quietly at first and gets louder over a few weeks. If you've only just noticed it, it's likely been building for a while.

Is a thumping dryer dangerous to keep using?

Not immediately, if it's just an unbalanced load. But a flat-spotted roller or worn bearing left unchecked can eventually let the drum sit unevenly, which increases wear on the motor and belt — worth checking sooner rather than later.

posts.post_title: Dishwasher Leaking Water? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Most dishwasher leaks trace back to a worn door seal, a loose water inlet connection, a cracked spray arm, or a blocked drain filter. Too much detergent (or the wrong type) is another common, often-overlooked cause. All are worth checking before assuming the whole machine needs replacing.

1. Check the door seal

The rubber gasket around the door is the most common source of a leak that shows up at the front of the machine. Run your hand around the inside of the seal for food residue, grit, or tears — a seal coated in grime often won't close properly even if it isn't damaged. Wipe it clean and check the door latches firmly before running another cycle.

2. Check the water inlet connection

At the front left or bottom of most dishwashers is where the water supply line connects. Pull the machine out carefully (power and water off first) and look for dampness around this fitting — a loose connection or a cracked inlet hose is a common cause of a slow leak that pools underneath rather than inside the machine.

3. Check the spray arm for cracks

The rotating spray arms can crack or develop small splits over time, especially near the centre mount. A cracked arm sprays water outward instead of onto the dishes, which can look like a leak from inside the tub. Spin each arm by hand and check for visible damage or a wobble at the mount point.

4. Check the drain and filter for blockages

A blocked filter or drain can cause water to back up and overflow rather than draining away properly. Most dishwashers have a removable filter at the bottom of the tub — take it out, clear off any food debris, and rinse it under a tap before refitting.

5. You might be using too much detergent

Too much detergent, the wrong type (dish soap instead of dishwasher detergent is a common mix-up), or a rinse-aid dispenser that's overfilled can all create excess suds that force water out around the door seal. If you're seeing foam as well as water, cut back the detergent dose and check the leak stops on the next cycle.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've checked the seal, inlet connection, spray arms and filter and the dishwasher is still leaking — especially from underneath, or if you notice a crack in the tub itself — it's likely a pump seal or tub fault that needs the machine opened up. Continuing to run a leaking dishwasher risks warping kitchen flooring and cabinetry. Our dishwasher repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A dishwasher leak rarely fixes itself — left unchecked, the water damage to flooring or cabinets often costs more to put right than the repair itself.

This is almost always a worn or dirty door seal, or occasionally excess suds from too much detergent forcing water past the seal. Clean the seal first and check your detergent dose before assuming the seal needs replacing.

Is it safe to keep using a leaking dishwasher?

For a small, identified leak you've already traced to something minor, it's usually fine to run one more load. But if the leak is coming from underneath, growing larger, or you're not sure of the source, stop using it — water near the electrics is a safety risk, and ongoing leaking can damage flooring and cabinetry.

posts.post_title: Fridge Leaking Water? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Most fridge leaks trace back to a blocked defrost drain, a torn or dirty door seal letting in humid air that condenses and drips, or a drip pan that's cracked or sitting out of place. All three take a few minutes to check yourself before booking a repair.

1. Check the defrost drain isn't blocked

Inside the freezer or at the back of the fridge compartment, a small drain channel carries defrost water down to a pan underneath. Food debris, ice or grime can block this drain, causing water to back up and leak inside the fridge or run out onto the floor. A pipe cleaner or a turkey baster of warm water can often clear a mild blockage.

2. Check the drip pan underneath

Most fridges have a small drip pan at the base that collects defrost water and lets it evaporate. If it's been knocked out of position, is cracked, or has simply filled up because it isn't evaporating fast enough in a humid room, water can overflow onto the floor. Pull the fridge out (unplugged) and check the pan is seated correctly and free of cracks.

3. Check the door seal

A worn, torn or dirty door gasket lets warm, humid air into the fridge, which condenses on the cold interior surfaces and can drip or pool at the bottom. Run your hand around the seal for tears, and check it's making full contact all the way around the door.

4. Check the water line (if you have an ice or water dispenser)

A loose or cracked connection where the water line enters the back of the fridge is a common source of leaks that show up as puddles behind or underneath the unit rather than inside it. Check the fitting is firmly connected and the line itself isn't kinked or split.

5. Make sure the fridge is level

A fridge that's tilted forward can stop water draining properly toward the drain channel and pan, causing it to pool and leak from the front instead. Use a spirit level across the top and adjust the front feet until it sits level or very slightly tilted back.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've checked the drain, drip pan, door seal and water line and the fridge is still leaking — or the leak is accompanied by the fridge running warm or making unusual noises — it's likely a cracked internal component or a sealed system fault that needs a proper diagnosis. Our fridge repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

Water pooling under or inside a fridge is worth acting on quickly — left unchecked, it can damage flooring and, in some cases, point to a fault that's also affecting cooling. See our guide on what to check if your fridge isn't cooling.

Why is there water pooling inside my fridge at the bottom?

This is almost always a blocked defrost drain — water that should drain away safely backs up and pools in the bottom of the fridge or crisper drawers instead. Clearing the drain channel usually resolves it.

Is a leaking fridge dangerous or urgent?

Not usually an emergency, but it's worth addressing promptly — ongoing water on the floor can damage flooring or cabinetry, and a leak combined with warm running temperatures can mean food safety is also at risk.

posts.post_content:
Quick answer: An oven that bakes unevenly — burnt on one side, raw on the other, or cooking faster at the back — is usually down to a faulty heating element, a fan that isn't running properly, a worn door seal, or overcrowded racks blocking airflow. Most of these are worth checking yourself before assuming the whole oven is broken.

1. Check the oven's actual temperature

The dial or display can drift out of calibration over the years, running hotter or cooler than it says. A cheap oven thermometer placed in the centre rack for a real preheat cycle will tell you if the oven is actually reaching (and holding) the temperature you've set — a surprisingly common and easy-to-miss cause of uneven results.

2. Check the fan is actually running (fan-forced ovens)

In a fan-forced or convection oven, the fan is what circulates hot air evenly around every rack. If the fan motor has failed or slowed down, heat pools at the top and stays cooler at the bottom — open the door partway during preheating (carefully) and listen or look for the fan actually spinning, not just the motor humming.

3. Check both heating elements are glowing (electric ovens)

Most electric ovens have a top grill element and a bottom bake element. If one has failed, the oven can still heat up and seem to "work" — just unevenly, since only one element is doing the work. Run the oven empty for a few minutes and visually check that both elements are glowing red.

4. Check the door seal

A torn, flattened or loose door gasket lets heat escape unevenly around the door, which can make the thermostat sensor read the temperature as correct while the far corners of the oven run noticeably cooler. Run your hand around the closed door while the oven's hot (carefully) to feel for escaping heat.

5. Check rack position and avoid overcrowding

Cooking on the middle rack gives the most even heat in most ovens, and multiple trays or dishes crowded in together block airflow between them, causing uneven results even in a perfectly working oven. Leave gaps around each tray and rotate trays halfway through longer bakes as good practice.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've confirmed the temperature is accurate, the fan's spinning, both elements are glowing and the door seal's intact — but baking is still uneven, or you notice one element not heating at all — it's likely a faulty element, thermostat or control board, and that's a job for a qualified technician. Our oven repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

An oven that runs hot in one spot and cool in another doesn't just ruin bakes — it can also mean a failing element is close to giving out completely.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my oven cook unevenly on one side?

This usually points to a fan that isn't circulating air properly, or a heating element that's only partially working. It's rarely a sign the whole oven needs replacing — both are common, fixable faults.

Can a faulty heating element cause uneven baking without the oven seeming "off"?

Yes — if only one of the two elements has failed, the oven still heats and the display still shows the set temperature, but with only half the heating capacity working evenly. It's one of the easiest oven faults to miss without checking visually.

posts.post_title: Fridge Making Noise? Here’s What It Means
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A steady hum or the occasional click from your fridge is normal — that's the compressor and thermostat cycling on and off. A loud buzzing, rattling or grinding noise is more often caused by uneven feet, something touching the back panel, or a fan struggling against an ice build-up, and is worth checking before it turns into a bigger fault.

1. A steady hum or gentle buzz

This is almost always the compressor running — a normal part of every fridge's cycle. It should sit at roughly the volume of a quiet conversation and cut in and out every 20–40 minutes, not run constantly at a noticeably louder volume.

2. Clicking when the fridge starts or stops

A single click as the compressor kicks in or shuts off is the start relay or thermostat doing its job — completely normal. Repeated clicking that doesn't lead to the compressor actually starting can mean the start relay or capacitor is failing.

3. Rattling or vibrating

Check that the fridge is sitting level — uneven feet are the most common cause of a rattle, especially on tiled or floating floors. Also check nothing (bottles, containers, the drip tray) is touching the back panel or coils, since vibration transfers easily through contact.

4. A loud buzz or whine from the back or the freezer

This is usually the condenser fan (at the back) or the evaporator fan (inside the freezer compartment) struggling against dust build-up or, more often, an ice build-up around the fan blade from a door not sealing properly. Defrosting the freezer fully for 24 hours often resolves it.

5. Popping, cracking or creaking

Normal, and more noticeable in newer fridges — it's the plastic internal panels expanding and contracting slightly as the temperature cycles. Nothing to worry about on its own.

When it's a job for a technician

If the noise is genuinely new, getting louder, or the fridge isn't holding temperature as well as it used to alongside the noise, it's worth having it looked at — a failing compressor or fan motor rarely fixes itself. Our fridge repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A fridge that's both noisy and running warmer than usual is the combination worth acting on quickly — see our guide on what to check if your fridge isn't cooling.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for a fridge to make some noise?

Yes — a steady hum and the occasional click as the compressor cycles on and off are completely normal. It's a sudden change in volume, pitch, or a new noise altogether that's worth paying attention to.

Why has my fridge suddenly gotten louder?

A sudden increase usually means either the fridge has come out of level, something is touching the back panel, or a fan is labouring against dust or ice build-up. Gradual, worsening noise over weeks points more towards a fan motor or compressor wearing out.

Can a noisy fridge still be cooling properly?

Often yes, at least for a while — noise and cooling faults don't always happen together. But a fan struggling against ice build-up will eventually affect cooling too, so it's worth checking rather than waiting for both problems to show up at once.
