posts.post_title: Washing Machine Not Spinning? 5 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A washing machine that fills and washes but won't spin is most often caused by an unbalanced load, a faulty door or lid lock, or a worn drive belt. If the drum is completely silent and won't even attempt to spin, check the door lock light and rebalance the load before assuming the worst — most of these faults are a five-minute fix.

1. Rebalance the load

A single heavy item — a doona, a pair of jeans, or a bunched-up towel — can throw the drum off balance enough to trigger a safety cut-out that stops the spin cycle entirely. Open the machine, redistribute the load evenly around the drum, and restart the spin cycle.

2. Check the door or lid lock

Front-loaders won't spin at all if the door lock hasn't engaged properly — look for a lock indicator light on the control panel. Top-loaders rely on a lid switch that can wear out or get knocked out of alignment over time. If the door feels loose or doesn't click firmly shut, that's usually your answer.

3. Make sure it isn't stuck on a wash or rinse cycle

Some machines pause the cycle and won't spin if the load is still soapy or hasn't fully drained between rinse stages. Let the full cycle run through rather than interrupting it, and check the drain hose isn't kinked or the filter isn't blocked (see the next point).

4. Check the drain pump filter

Most front-loaders have an accessible filter near the bottom front of the machine. A pump filter clogged with coins, hair ties or lint can stop the machine progressing to the spin stage at all, since it won't spin a drum that hasn't drained. Clear it out and try again.

5. Listen for the drive belt (top-loaders and older machines)

If the drum spins freely by hand but the machine won't spin on its own, or you hear the motor running without the drum moving, a worn or snapped drive belt is a common cause. It's a straightforward part to replace but does need the machine opened up.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've rebalanced the load, confirmed the door's locking properly, and the machine still won't spin — or it's spinning but making a grinding noise or a burning smell — the motor, control board or suspension may be at fault, and that's best left to a qualified technician. Our washing machine repair technicians in Hobart diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

A machine that keeps trying to spin but can't will wear the motor and bearings faster, so it's worth getting looked at sooner rather than running load after load.

Why does my washing machine fill and wash but not spin?

This almost always points to the spin-stage safety checks failing — an unbalanced load, a door that hasn't locked, or a blocked drain filter preventing the machine from confirming it's safe to spin. Work through the checks above in order.

Not usually — the belt itself is an inexpensive part. Most of the cost is the labour to access it, since it typically means removing the back or base panel. We'll always quote this upfront before starting.

posts.post_title: Vacuum Losing Suction? Here's What to Check Before Booking a Repair
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Sudden loss of suction is almost always caused by a full bin or bag, a clogged filter, or something tangled in the brush roll or blocking the hose — all fixable in a few minutes without tools. If suction is weak even with everything clean and clear, or you notice a burning smell, that points to a failing motor and needs a technician rather than a DIY fix.

1. Empty the bin or check the bag

It sounds obvious, but a bin that's more than about two-thirds full — or a bag that's compacted rather than genuinely full — will noticeably reduce suction well before it looks "full" to the eye. Empty it and give the bin itself a wipe out, since fine dust can coat the inside and restrict airflow even when it looks empty.

2. Clean or replace the filters

Most vacuums have at least one washable filter, and some (especially bagless models) have two or three. A clogged filter is one of the most common causes of gradually worsening suction. Check your manual for which filters are washable, rinse them with water only (no detergent), and let them dry fully — at least 24 hours — before refitting.

3. Check the brush roll for tangled hair and thread

Hair, thread and carpet fibres wind tightly around the brush roll over time, eventually stopping it from spinning freely and forcing the motor to work harder for less suction. Turn the vacuum over, remove the brush roll cover, and cut away any tangled material with scissors — be careful of the bristles.

4. Check the hose and attachments for blockages

Small toys, cotton balls and bits of paper are common culprits for a partial or full blockage inside the hose. Detach the hose and look (or feel) through it for anything stuck, and check the point where the hose connects to the main body too.

5. Check the belt (upright and bagged vacuums)

If the brush roll isn't spinning at all even with nothing tangled in it, the drive belt may have snapped or slipped off. This is visible once you remove the brush roll cover, and on many models it's a straightforward, inexpensive part to replace.

When it's a job for a technician

If the bin's empty, the filters are clean, the brush roll spins freely and there's nothing blocking the hose — but suction is still weak, or you notice a burning smell, unusual noise, or the motor cutting out — the motor itself is likely failing, or on cyclone-style vacuums (like Dyson) there may be a cracked cyclone assembly losing seal. For cordless vacuums, a battery that no longer holds charge can also look like a suction problem. Our vacuum repair technicians in Hobart service most major brands, including Dyson, and diagnose the fault with upfront pricing before any work begins.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why has my vacuum suddenly lost suction?

A sudden drop (rather than a gradual decline) is usually a blockage — something stuck in the hose or brush roll — rather than a worn-out motor. Gradual, ongoing loss of suction over weeks or months more often points to a clogged filter or an ageing motor.

Is it worth repairing a vacuum or should I just replace it?

For mid-range and premium vacuums (including most Dyson and similar models), repair is usually well worth it — motors, batteries and cyclone assemblies can often be replaced individually for a fraction of the cost of a new unit. We'll always give you an honest opinion on whether repair or replacement makes more sense for your model.

posts.post_title: Dryer Not Drying Clothes? 4 Things to Check
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: A dryer that's taking far longer than usual to dry a load — or running warm but never quite finishing — is almost always caused by a blocked lint filter or vent, an overloaded drum, or a build-up of fabric softener residue on the moisture sensor. All of these are quick DIY checks. If the dryer runs but the air coming out is cold, or the drum isn't turning at all, that's a heating element, thermal fuse or belt fault and needs a technician.

1. Clean the lint filter — every single load

A lint filter that's even partially clogged chokes airflow and can double or triple drying times. Pull it out, peel off the lint by hand, and give it a wash under warm water every few weeks — fabric softener sheets leave a waxy film that a quick wipe won't remove.

2. Check the vent hose for blockages (and check for fire risk)

The flexible hose running from the back of the dryer to the outside wall is the single biggest cause of long drying times — and a genuine fire hazard when it's badly blocked. Disconnect it (dryer off and unplugged) and check for kinks, crushed sections, or a build-up of lint at the outside vent flap. If you haven't cleaned this vent in over a year, it's worth doing regardless of whether you're having problems.

3. Don't overload the drum

Clothes need room to tumble freely for hot air to reach them. A drum packed to the top will take much longer to dry evenly, and heavy items (towels, jeans) are best dried in smaller loads on their own.

4. Wipe down the moisture sensor strips

Most modern dryers have two small metal sensor strips inside the drum that detect when clothes are dry. Fabric softener and dryer sheets leave a residue on these strips over time, which can make the dryer think clothes are dry (or never dry) when they're not. Wipe them with a cloth and some rubbing alcohol.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've cleaned the filter and vent, aren't overloading the drum, and the dryer is still taking forever — or worse, running with only cold air, or the drum has stopped turning while the motor still hums — the fault is likely a burnt-out heating element, a tripped thermal fuse, or a broken drive belt. A dryer that's lost heat entirely and one that's stopped turning both need the cabinet opened up, and a persistent vent blockage combined with continued use is one of the more common causes of house fires, so it's not worth pushing through. Our dryer repair technicians in Hobart diagnose most of these faults on the first visit, with upfront pricing before any work begins.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my dryer run but not heat?

This is almost always a blown thermal fuse or a burnt-out heating element. The thermal fuse is a safety device that cuts heat (but not the motor) if the dryer overheats — often triggered by a blocked vent — so it's worth checking your vent even after a repair to stop it happening again.

Is a dryer that takes forever to dry a fire risk?

It can be. Long drying times are frequently a symptom of a blocked lint vent, and blocked dryer vents are one of the most common causes of house fires involving appliances. If cleaning the filter and vent doesn't fix it, get it checked rather than continuing to run longer cycles.

posts.post_title: Dishwasher Not Draining? How to Fix It (or Know When to Call a Repair Tech)
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Standing water in the bottom of a dishwasher after a cycle is almost always one of three things — a clogged filter basket, a kinked or blocked drain hose, or (if you've recently had a garbage disposal or new sink fitted) a knockout plug that was never removed from the drain line. All three are checkable in a few minutes without tools. If the pump is humming loudly but nothing drains, that's a motor fault and needs a technician.

1. Clean out the filter basket

Almost every dishwasher has a removable filter assembly at the bottom of the tub, usually a twist-lock cylinder in one corner. Food scraps, labels and broken glass build up here over time and are the single most common cause of poor draining. Twist it out, rinse it thoroughly under the tap, and clear any debris from the recess it sits in before replacing it.

2. Check the drain hose for kinks or blockages

The corrugated drain hose runs from the back of the dishwasher to either the sink's drain pipe or the garbage disposal. If the dishwasher's been moved, or cabinetry work has been done nearby, the hose can end up kinked or pinched behind the unit. Pull the dishwasher out carefully and check the hose runs in a smooth loop with no tight bends.

3. Check the air gap or disposal knockout plug

If your dishwasher drains through an air gap fitting on the sink, check it isn't clogged — unscrew the cap and clear any buildup. If it connects to a garbage disposal unit, and that disposal was installed or replaced recently, there's a knockout plug inside the disposal's inlet that has to be removed for the dishwasher to drain — it's a very common miss during installation.

4. Don't overdo the rinse aid or use the wrong detergent

Using dish soap instead of dishwasher detergent, or too much rinse aid, creates excess foam that can overwhelm the drain pump and leave water sitting in the tub. If you've noticed suds along with the standing water, that's your answer — switch products and run an empty cycle to clear it.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've cleared the filter, checked the hose and the air gap or disposal plug, and there's still water sitting in the bottom — especially if you can hear the pump humming or straining without anything draining — the drain pump motor, a check valve, or the control board has likely failed. Standing water left in a dishwasher can also start to smell and encourage mould around the door seal, so it's worth getting looked at sooner rather than later. Our dishwasher repair technicians in Hobart diagnose most drainage faults on the first visit, with upfront pricing before any work begins.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is there standing water in the bottom of my dishwasher?

Most often it's a clogged filter basket or a kinked/blocked drain hose. If the dishwasher was recently connected to a new garbage disposal, check that the disposal's knockout plug was removed — it's a common installation miss that stops draining completely.

Can I run my dishwasher if it's not draining properly?

We wouldn't recommend it. Running a cycle on top of standing water won't clean dishes properly, can make the smell and mould risk worse, and if the cause is a failing pump motor, continuing to run it can burn the motor out completely.

posts.post_title: Oven Not Heating Up? 5 Things to Check Before Calling a Technician
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: If your oven turns on but won't heat, start with the simple things — a tripped circuit breaker, the wrong cooking mode selected, a door that isn't closing fully, or (for gas ovens) an igniter that isn't sparking. If the oven powers on normally, the display works, and it still won't heat after these checks, the heating element, igniter or thermostat has likely failed — and that's an electrical or gas repair, not a DIY job.

1. Check the circuit breaker first

Ovens draw a lot of power, and a partially tripped breaker can sometimes leave the display and oven light working while cutting power to the heating circuit itself. Check your switchboard and reset the relevant breaker fully off, then on.

2. Make sure you're on the right mode

It sounds obvious, but on ovens with separate bake, grill and fan-forced settings, it's easy to accidentally select grill only (which won't heat the main oven cavity the same way) or leave it on a timed/delay setting that's holding off the actual heating cycle. Double check the mode dial or display against the manual.

3. Check the door is closing and sealing fully

Many ovens have a safety interlock that reduces or cuts heating if the door isn't detected as fully closed. Check nothing (a tray, glove, or food residue) is stopping the door from closing completely, and inspect the rubber door seal for gaps, tears or flattening.

4. Self-clean lockout

If your oven has a self-cleaning function, some models lock the door and disable normal heating for a period after a self-clean cycle as a safety measure. If you've run self-clean recently, check the manual for how long the lockout lasts.

5. Look (don't touch) for visible element or igniter damage

With the oven off and cool, you can visually check the heating element (electric ovens) for obvious blistering, a break in the coil, or scorch marks — signs it has burnt out. On gas ovens, listen for the igniter clicking when you turn the oven on; if you hear gas but no ignition, or no clicking at all, the igniter has likely failed. Don't attempt to test or replace either yourself — both involve mains electricity or a live gas supply.

When it's a job for a technician

A burnt-out heating element, a failed igniter, a faulty thermostat or a control board fault are the most common causes of an oven that powers on but won't heat — and all four require a qualified technician, both for safety and because Australian gas fitting work legally has to be done by a licensed person. Keep using an oven with a suspected element or igniter fault and you risk it not heating evenly, tripping the circuit repeatedly, or in gas ovens, a build-up of unburnt gas. Our oven repair technicians in Hobart carry the most common element, igniter and thermostat parts on the van, so most faults are fixed on the first visit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is my oven not heating but the light still works?

The oven light and display run on a much lower-power circuit than the heating element or igniter, so it's common for the light and controls to work perfectly fine while the actual heating fault sits elsewhere — usually the element, igniter, thermostat or control board.

Is it dangerous to keep using an oven that won't heat properly?

If it's genuinely not heating at all, the main risk is food safety (undercooked food) rather than danger. But if it's heating unevenly, cycling on and off unexpectedly, tripping your breaker, or you can smell gas on a gas oven, stop using it and get it looked at — those are signs of a fault that can get worse.

It depends on the part needed — element and thermostat replacements are generally the most affordable, while control board faults cost more. See our appliance repair cost guide for what typically affects the price, or we'll diagnose and quote upfront before any work starts.

posts.post_title: Washing Machine Leaking Water? 5 Things to Check Before You Call a Repairman
posts.post_content:
Quick answer: Most washing machine leaks trace back to one of four things — a torn or dirty door seal, a clogged drain filter, a loose hose connection, or too much detergent creating oversudsing. All four take under 10 minutes to check yourself. If the leak shows up mid-cycle from underneath the machine, or comes with a grinding or knocking noise, that's usually a drain pump or tub bearing fault, and it's a job for a technician rather than a DIY fix.

1. Check the door seal (front loaders)

The rubber gasket around a front-loading washing machine's door is the most common source of leaks. Run your hand around the inside fold of the seal — coins, hair ties, and grit often get trapped in the lower crease and stop the door from sealing properly. Wipe it clean, check for tears or flattened sections, and make sure nothing is caught in the door latch itself.

2. Inspect the drain pump filter

Almost every washing machine has a small access panel near the bottom front of the unit that hides the drain pump filter. If this filter is clogged with lint, coins or a stray sock, water can back up and leak out around it. Turn the machine off, place a shallow tray underneath, and unscrew the filter slowly — it will usually still have some water behind it. Clear out any debris and check the filter's own seal (a rubber O-ring) isn't cracked before screwing it back in.

3. Check the inlet and outlet hoses

Pull the machine out from the wall (unplug it first) and look at both the cold/hot water inlet hoses at the back and the corrugated drain hose. Hand-tighten any loose hose clamps, and check the drain hose isn't kinked, cracked, or pushed in so far it's sitting in standing water — that alone can cause siphoning and leaks during the cycle.

4. You might be using too much detergent

Front loaders in particular need far less detergent than older top-loading machines, and using a top-loader amount (or the wrong type of detergent) creates excess suds that can force water out around the door seal or detergent drawer. If you're seeing foam as well as water, cut your detergent dose in half and see if the leak stops on the next wash.

5. Check it's sitting level

An unlevel machine can rock during the spin cycle, which stresses hose connections and seals over time. Use a spirit level on top of the machine and adjust the front feet until it's flat and stable in both directions.

When it's a job for a technician

If you've worked through the checks above and the machine is still leaking — especially if the leak appears from underneath mid-cycle, gets worse over time, or is accompanied by grinding, banging or a burning smell — it's most likely a failed drain pump, a cracked outer tub, or worn tub bearings. These are internal faults that need the machine opened up, and continuing to run a machine with a bearing or pump fault can damage the motor and the floor underneath it. Frequently Asked Questions

Is it safe to keep using a leaking washing machine?

For a small, identified leak (like a loose hose clamp) it's usually fine to run one more load while you source a part. But if the leak is coming from underneath, growing larger, or you can smell burning, stop using the machine — water near the motor and electrics is a safety risk, not just a mess.

Can a leaking washing machine be fixed the same day?

Often, yes. Door seals, drain pump filters and hose faults are usually straightforward repairs our technicians can complete in a single visit. Drain pump or bearing replacements can sometimes need a part ordered in, which we'll confirm at diagnosis.

It depends on the fault — a hose or filter fix costs far less than a drain pump or bearing replacement. See our appliance repair cost guide for what typically affects the price, or we'll diagnose and quote upfront before any work starts.

posts.post_content:
A fridge that's not cooling properly is one of the most common calls we get in Hobart — and the good news is that a surprising number of these faults are things you can rule out yourself before booking a technician.

If it's actually the freezer compartment that's not cold rather than the fridge side, see our guide on freezer not freezing.

1. Check the door seal first

A worn or dirty door seal (gasket) is the single most common reason a fridge struggles to stay cold. Close the door on a piece of paper — if you can pull the paper out easily, the seal isn't holding properly. Wipe the gasket down with warm soapy water; food residue and grime are often the real culprit, not a faulty seal.

2. Give the coils a clean

The condenser coils, usually at the back or underneath the fridge, radiate heat away from the unit. When they're covered in a season's worth of dust and pet hair, the compressor has to work much harder — and sometimes can't keep up. Unplug the fridge and vacuum the coils every six months or so.

3. Check the temperature setting

It sounds obvious, but a knock to the dial (or a curious toddler) is more common than you'd think. Fridges should sit between 3°C and 5°C, and freezers at -18°C.

4. Don't overpack it

Cold air needs to circulate. A fridge packed floor to ceiling after a big shop can't maintain even temperatures, and food near the door can sit several degrees warmer than the back.

When it's time to call a technician

If you've checked all of the above and the fridge still isn't cooling, or you're hearing unusual noises, seeing ice buildup, or noticing water pooling underneath, it's likely a compressor, thermostat or refrigerant issue — and that's a job for a qualified technician rather than a DIY fix. posts.post_content:
Last updated: September 2026

Hobart Appliance Care ("we," "us," "our") repairs household appliances — fridges, washing machines, ovens, dishwashers, dryers and vacuums — for customers across Hobart, Launceston, Burnie, Devonport, Ulverstone and greater Tasmania. This Privacy Policy explains what personal information we collect when you book a repair or use this website, why we collect it, and the choices you have.

1. Information We Collect

When you submit a booking request through our website, we collect the details needed to send a technician to your property, including:

  • Your name, phone number and email address
  • Your property address (street address and suburb), so a technician can attend
  • Property type (e.g. house, unit, rental)
  • The appliance brand, model, and a description of the problem
  • Warranty and retailer details, where relevant to your repair
  • A preferred appointment time
  • An onsite contact's name and phone number, if you are booking on behalf of someone else at the property (for example, a landlord or property manager booking for a tenant)

We also automatically collect some technical information when you browse our website, such as your IP address, browser type, device type, and pages viewed, through cookies and standard website analytics.

2. How We Use Your Information

  • To arrange, schedule and carry out your appliance repair, including sending a technician to your address
  • To send you a confirmation of your booking request by email
  • To contact you about your appointment, quote, or an active repair
  • To process warranty claims where you have asked us to liaise with a retailer or manufacturer
  • To maintain records for invoicing, our 12-month workmanship guarantee, and legitimate business record-keeping
  • To improve our website and service

3. How We Share Information

We do not sell your personal information. Booking details are sent by email to our own business inbox and handled by our technicians and administrative staff for the purpose of carrying out your repair. We also rely on service providers to operate our business, including:

  • Website hosting provider — which stores and processes our website and the email delivery of your booking request
  • Retailers or manufacturers — only where you have asked us to action a warranty claim on your behalf

We only disclose personal information to others where required by law, or with your consent.

4. Bookings Made on Behalf of Someone Else

If you are a landlord, property manager, or otherwise booking a repair for a property where you do not live, you confirm that you are authorised to arrange the visit and to share the onsite contact's name and phone number with us so our technician can coordinate access.

5. Cookies

We use cookies for essential website functionality, performance (caching), and basic analytics to understand how visitors use our site. You can control or disable cookies in your browser settings, though parts of the site may not function as intended if you do.

6. Data Retention

We keep your booking and job information for as long as necessary to complete your repair, honour our 12-month guarantee, and meet our record-keeping and tax obligations, after which it is deleted or de-identified where we no longer need it.

7. Your Rights

Under the Australian Privacy Principles, you can ask us:

  • What personal information we hold about you
  • To correct information that is inaccurate or out of date
  • To delete personal information we no longer need to hold

To make a request, contact us using the details in Section 9. If you are not satisfied with our response, you may contact the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) at oaic.gov.au.

8. Data Security

We take reasonable steps to protect the personal information we hold, including your property address and contact details, from misuse, loss, or unauthorised access. No method of storage or transmission over the internet is completely secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security.

9. Contact Us

Questions about this Privacy Policy or your personal information can be sent to:

  • Email: bookings@hobartappliancecare.com
  • Phone: bookings@hobartappliancecare.com
  • Address: Hobart, TAS 7000, Australia

10. Changes to This Policy

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. The "Last updated" date at the top of this page shows when it was last revised.
